extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate or graduate students in mathematical logic / computability theory
extracted.subtask_description: A multi-week course project with reading and problem exercises on primitive recursive, general recursive, and Turing computable functions aimed at understanding Church's thesis via primary sources (Gödel, Kleene, Turing). Students read excerpts, rewrite formal schemata, construct/justify Turing machines, and prove preservation/closure properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze Gödel's initial rejection and Turing's influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze Kurt Gödel’s initial rejection of Church’s thesis and the work of Alan Turing that finally convinced Gödel of the validity of Church’s thesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study primary historical sources by Gödel, Kleene, and Turing; explain historical narrative and technical reasons given in the primary texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict attention to total functions
rubrics_metrics.description: For this project, restrict attention to total functions (do not work with partial functions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The project will cover primitive recursive, general recursive, and Turing computable total functions; references are provided for partial-function results omitted here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show every general recursive function is Turing computable
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine Turing’s and Kleene’s definitions and show that every general recursive function is computable on a Turing machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The converse (every Turing computable function is general recursive) requires Gödel-number techniques and is not addressed fully here; refer to [5],[6],[11],[16] for full proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read and understand Gödel's schemata for recursion (schemes (1) and (2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully read Gödel’s excerpt defining compound/recursive functions and the two schemata (1) and (2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to work with the formal statements: substitution (scheme (1)) and recursion (scheme (2)); the project chooses the reprinted version for convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite and explain Gödel's rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite rule (1) for n=1 and m=2, and rewrite rule (2) for n=1. Explain in your own words what the rules express.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tests ability to manipulate the formal schemata and to articulate their informal meaning; explicitly perform the substitutions and describe the resulting operational behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define primitive recursive functions in own words
rubrics_metrics.description: Give a definition of primitive recursive functions in your own words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Gödel’s and Kleene’s schemata (successor, constant, identity, substitution, primitive recursion) to motivate the definition; compare with Kleene's later formulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argue that basic arithmetic functions are primitive recursive
rubrics_metrics.description: Give an argument for why the functions Gödel lists (Gödel: "The functions x C y, xy, xy and xŠ are clearly [primitive] recursive.") are primitive recursive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review your definition of primitive recursion and show how addition, multiplication, exponentiation (and other listed functions) are obtained from base functions via substitution and primitive recursion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether every function is primitive recursive
rubrics_metrics.description: Answer: Is every function of natural numbers primitive recursive? (Hint: Use a cardinality argument.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the standard cardinality/counting argument showing there are more functions N->N than primitive recursive definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relate Gödel's remark about finite procedures to Church's thesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain any connection between Gödel’s statement 'the value of the function can be computed by a finite procedure' and Church’s thesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss heuristic/semantic alignment between Gödel's informally stated effective calculability and Church's formal identifications (lambda-definability/general recursiveness/Turing computability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare your primitive-recursive definition to Kleene's
rubrics_metrics.description: Is your answer to 1.(c) equivalent to Kleene’s definition of primitive recursive functions? Explain why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read Kleene’s schemata (I)-(V) and show equivalence or explain differences; use explicit translation between formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand total vs partial functions and the μ-operator
rubrics_metrics.description: Recall definitions of total and partial functions; read Kleene's definition of the (μ)-operator and discuss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give an example of a function obtainable by the μ-operator that is not total; explain the role of condition (3) (a boundedness/uniqueness condition) in guaranteeing totality when (3) holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define general recursive functions using Kleene's schemata
rubrics_metrics.description: Based on Kleene’s Theorem III and corollary, give a definition of general recursive functions and explain whether every primitive recursive function is general recursive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use closure under Schemata (I)–(VI) with condition (3) for (VI) to formulate the class; show primitive recursive ⊆ general recursive via the schemata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether every function is general recursive
rubrics_metrics.description: Is every function of natural numbers general recursive? Explain your answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use diagonalization/cardinality arguments or other standard computability-theoretic reasons to argue existence of non-general-recursive functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argue that general recursive strictly extends primitive recursive (extra credit)
rubrics_metrics.description: (Extra Credit) Give a reasonable argument for why the class of general recursive functions is strictly larger than the class of primitive recursive functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical approach: exhibit a total general recursive function that is not primitive recursive (e.g., use μ-operator to define the Ackermann-like behaviors) or invoke existence of functions provably not primitive recursive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe Turing machine components and configurations
rubrics_metrics.description: What are the primary components of a Turing machine? Describe m-configurations, configurations, and complete configurations and their differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Turing's exposition: tape, squares, symbols, scanned square, m-configurations (machine states), conﬁgurations (state + scanned symbol), and complete configurations (state + tape contents + scanned position).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulate Turing's definitions of computing machine/sequence/real
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulate in your own words Turing’s definition of a computing machine, a computable sequence (of natural numbers), and a computable real number (in [0,1]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain circle-free vs circular machines, distinguishing symbols of the first kind (figures 0 and 1) used for the output sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct simple Turing machines and justify correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand Turing's example machines (e.g., machine that computes 010101...) and design your own (e.g., compute real 1/7). Provide an argument for why the machine does what it is supposed to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe states, scanned symbols, table of operations, and give stepwise reasoning or sample complete configurations demonstrating correct output behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain use of auxiliary symbols in Turing machines
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the need for symbols of the second kind (e.g., '@' and 'x') in constructing certain Turing machines and argue why the described machine produces the intended sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss how second-kind symbols serve as temporary markers, 'keep place' values, or scratchwork that are later erased, and show via configuration tables how they enable the computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain Turing's definition of computable functions (sequence-to-function mapping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain Turing’s definition of computable functions of natural numbers based on computable sequences where counts between zeros encode values: (Turing's construction mapping sequences to number-theoretic functions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restate: if α is a computable sequence with infinitely many 0s, define f(n) as number of 1s between nth and (n+1)th zero; such f is Turing computable.

rubrics_metrics.name: State what it means for a function to be Turing computable (one-variable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain in your own words what it means for a function of natural numbers of one variable to be Turing computable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extra credit: generalize to two or more variables (hint: encode tuples as single numbers or use delimiter/tally encodings on the tape).

rubrics_metrics.name: Read and restate Kleene’s formal definition of a Turing machine
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain Kleene’s definition of a Turing machine (tape symbols, machine states, atomic acts, moves) and how a machine's operation is specified by a table of acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be able to translate between Turing's intuitive descriptions and Kleene's formal table notation (sb L qd ; sb C qd ; sb R qd etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain Kleene’s definition of Turing-computable functions of multiple variables
rubrics_metrics.description: State in your own words Kleene’s definition of how a machine computes a partial/total number-theoretic function of n variables using tally representations separated by blanks and standard-position scanning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain representation conventions (tally groups, blanks before/after, standard position on last tally), why representation requires x1+1 squares, and the halting/standard-position output condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare Turing's and Kleene's definitions; assess equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain similarities and differences of Turing’s and Kleene’s definitions of machines and computability. Are they equivalent? Which do you prefer and why?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss formal equivalence proofs and pragmatic clarity; cite how both capture same intuitive 'mechanical' computation and how Kleene formalizes tape/symbol/state conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove basic functions are Turing computable
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why the successor function s(x)=x+1, constant functions, and identity functions U^n_j(x1,..,xn)=xj are Turing computable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct simple machines (or describe algorithmic tapes/states) that output the successor, constant, or copy an input under the tally encoding conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show substitution preserves Turing computability
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why if g and h1,...,hm are Turing computable then f(x1,..,xn)=g(h1(...),...,hm(...)) is Turing computable (schema of substitution preserves Turing computability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline how to combine machines (simulate submachines, use delimiters/trackwork) to compute composition and produce the combined output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show primitive recursion preserves Turing computability
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why primitive recursion schema preserves Turing computability: if base and step functions are Turing computable then the function defined by primitive recursion is Turing computable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe iterative simulation using the Turing machines for base and step functions to compute successive values and halt with final result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show μ-operator preserves Turing computability under condition (3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why if R(x1,..,xn,y) is Turing computable and condition (3) holds (existence/uniqueness/boundedness), then the function defined by μy R(...) is Turing computable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that a Turing machine can search incrementally for the least y satisfying R, and condition (3) guarantees termination/totality where required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduce relationship between primitive and general recursive functions and Church's thesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the exercises (5.a–5.f), deduce conclusions about primitive recursive and general recursive functions and relate these conclusions to Church’s thesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize that primitive recursive ⊆ general recursive ⊆ Turing computable (and vice versa under established equivalences), and explain how these formal equivalences provide evidence for Church’s thesis.
